facts.text: The family rents a movie on a video cassette and feeds it into the machine beneath the television.
A blinking clock on the video recorder often shows the wrong time after a power outage.
A child rewinds a rented videotape before taking it back to the shop.
The television remote disappears between sofa cushions just when someone wants to change channels.
Cable television brings extra channels to households that subscribe where service is available.
A rooftop antenna still brings broadcast television to homes without cable service.
Children gather around a television to play games using wired controllers.
A teenager carries a portable cassette player and listens through foam-covered headphones.
A car stereo may chew up a cassette tape and leave its ribbon tangled.
Families keep stacks of vinyl records beside their stereo cabinets.
A compact disc player appears in some homes later in the decade, though many families still play records and tapes.
A student copies a favorite song from the radio onto a blank cassette.
A corded telephone stretches from the kitchen wall while someone tries to talk privately.
Many households still use rotary telephones, while push-button models become increasingly familiar.
An answering machine records messages on a small cassette when nobody picks up the telephone.
A caller uses a pay telephone and keeps coins ready in case the call runs long.
An office worker types letters on a typewriter and corrects mistakes with correction fluid or tape.
Office staff make copies on a photocopier and clear paper jams when the machine stops.
A clerk feeds paper into a dot-matrix printer and hears its loud buzzing.
A home computer may connect to the family television or a separate monitor.
Children load some computer games from floppy disks or cassette tapes.
A computer owner saves schoolwork onto a floppy disk and keeps the disk away from magnets.
A household computer often runs programs from disks without any internet connection.
A cashier scans barcodes at some supermarkets, while smaller shops may still enter prices by hand.
A shopper waits while a clerk runs a credit card through a manual imprint machine.
A microwave oven heats leftovers quickly, and family members learn which dishes are safe to put inside.
A camera owner drops a roll of film at a photo counter and returns later for prints.
A pocket calculator sits beside a shopkeeper's ledger for checking totals.
